speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And you really know that you were the first white child ... ?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: My mother was.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Your mother was the first white child born in Latah County?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: In Latah, yes. [Narrator is showing some photographs.] And now, my great grandchild and my granddaughter in Seattle. She seems in a pretty good family. But this cabin, this is where I got that, this is still standing there. It's real worn down, but this is still standing there.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: There have been several pictures of that that they got in that pioneer book, you know.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Does your family still own the land that the cabin's on?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I sold it. On that land over there, there was a great old homestead. First, I want to show you. See, my uncle's brother-in-law lives over there [unintelligible].

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: This is my grandfather and his second marriage to her. There's my mother when she was 23, here she is again when she's older, and here's the fourth generation. My grandfather, my uncle and cousin and their daughter. And there is my grandson.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Here is my 50th birthday cake. Here I am with my son-in-law's cattle in Colton. They have a fine dairy down here. Here I am greeting people in a booth down there in Moscow ...

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: At the fair.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That's a good idea, isn't it?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh yeah. My pictures in our family [unintelligible] and I only got two of them.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Oh yes, of course.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: There's one of them. There's my daughter's son and teacher talking to me. [Unintelligible.] This is Grandpa's old fashion ice cream. It's a Safeway parking lot now.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Oh, is that right? What a shame.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: It was just a house, just a big house in Moscow.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And that was on the Safeway parking lot?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, and we had it right across from the Safeway parking lot there, the Roger's Ice Cream parlor. There's the five and dime here. But, when my grandfather [unintelligible] real common place. You had to [unintelligible].

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: So, they [unintel ligible] Spokane [unintelligible] and they come down and he took those pictures for me.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: A lot of people have interviewed you. We'd like to ask you some questions to get some kind of different information.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, I see, uh huh.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, we'll start off so I'll be sure to get your name right and everything. What is your full name?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Agnes Hailey Jones. That's the way I sign all my papers and everything.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And your maiden name was?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Agnes Hailey.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you have any nicknames?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: They always call me Ag.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Would you like to tell us what day you were born?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: January 16, 1890, out here.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And your address is just Genesee?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Just Genesee, Route 2, [unintelligible]. I just had to leave my husband in the rest home. I couldn't take care of him anymore, he was 95. It's just hospital care around the clock, you, know, you can't do it out here.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You were born in Genesee?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Out east, out west of here, northwest of Genesee, in a rustic cabin. I got a picture of that, too.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And your very, well, you just told me your very first residence in Idaho was in a log cabin.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, I was born in a log cabin, a rustic cabin. My father laid in the other corner of the room with a fractured led. Talk about hard times.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You were born when your father was lying in the corner of the room?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: His leg was hanged up from the ceiling, elevated, you know.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What kind of accident did he have?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, he rode off a haystack. See, they were just in the wood, you know, and they were milking cows. They had the fresh milk right here in Genesee and he delivered milk in town. So, Mother was up getting something out for the men who gave the cows and she heard noises and smelled cold weather, you know, smelly weather and foggy.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: So, she heard something and seen him roll right down over the haystack and broke his leg. He had to lay there till she run a mile and get somebody else. That was a month before I was born.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Oh, for heaven's sakes!

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: He laid there, thought they was_ going to save his foot; but, they didn't save it. He laid there from December until March, I guess, and they took him to Spokane and had to amputate his leg.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you know your mother's maiden name?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Annie M. Tierney.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you know what date she was born?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: October 15, 1871, in Thorn Creek, over here in Thorn Creek. First white girl ever born between Moscow and Lewiston.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: When did she die?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: In 1954, March the 17th. She fractured her hip and then she died. She was in a rest home and she slipped down off the bed. My granddaughter was looking after her and that's what happened.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What year was she married?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did she ever do anything besides work in the house or on the farm?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, she did all kinds of work on the farm. Them days, the men used to take what they call their grub box and tools and gear and horses and they used to go up and cut all their winter wood out. Then they used to mow down all these big trees, it was all timberland on this side of Troy. They'd mow them all down and make fences out of them, these rails, 16 feet long, these long fences.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: My dad would only stay two or three days at a time. And then, she had about 25 head of hogs to carry water to and she had to milk cows and she was a little person about 105 pounds, that's all. And she wasn't nearly 20 yet.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Oh, my.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, she had lots of hardships.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, she just stayed at home and worked on the farm?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, just stayed at home and maintained the farm and then she made lots of butter to sell. Genesee was new then and Dad delivered milk and she had butter customers. She had her own butter maker.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How about your father's family?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: He's from County Kerry, Ireland. He was born, I think, in 1837. I know he was about 97 when he died. He was about 44 years old when he got married.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And when did he die?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: He did lumbering?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, farming, that's all. And cattle raising. He always raised hogs and cattle.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you have brothers and sisters?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I had three sisters: Margaret, Laura and Ethel.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And no brothers. Now, your husband's name?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Harding B. Jones.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And what is his date of birth?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What has been his occupation?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, first, before we come here, he was a construction foreman on the streetcar streets and many motormen were on the streetcars [unintelligible] on the Spokane Treasury and Company in Spokane before we came down here again. See, I lived here until I was about 15. Then, I left my home and we were living over here in town and then I went away and worked for a while. Then I got married and then we come down here again in the fall and we've stayed here ever since.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I raised poultry, my goodness, I've got pictures of all kinds of poultry. I've even dressed them and everything, cured the feathers. Oh, it's hard, I tell you, on the ranch; it's a lot of hard work there.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And where was he born?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: He was born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And were you married here?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: We were married in Spokane.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And what date?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And he is still living?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, he's just at the rest home right now. He has to have nurse's care around the clock. He's 95 now.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How often do you get to see him?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, whenever somebody goes up, I get a ride. But, it isn't so bad. It gives him a chance to, well, you know.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How many children do you have?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I have three daughters.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And their names?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Eva Amos, Thelma Maria and Mary Agnes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Were they born here in Genesee?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Two were born in Spokane and one born in Colfax.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Eva was born in Spokane?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, and Thelma was born in Spokane. We lived up there then, and Mary was born over in Colfax.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Are they housewives?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, Eva, she's retired from work now and she was a meat wrapper. Well, she was a secretary for six and a half years down here at the Lewiston Grain. Then she got to be a meat wrapper. She had to belong to quite a few butcher's unions.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Her husband is a salesman for the Higrade people in Seattle, one of the top salesmen. And then, the second oldest girl, her and her husband have that dairy down here near Colton. Then, the youngest girl, she's a Home Ee teacher in the Seattle schools and Edmonton, Washington. Then, she has a business of her own, you know, fabrics.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: She has customers come to her home. She has a big job and she makes good money.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: All right. Did you go to high school?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How far did you go?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: About to the eighth grade and that's about all.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Have you always been a homemaker on the farm?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. When I lived in Spokane before I was married, I tell you, I worked in the grocery stores. Then, I cooked hotcakes and waffles two and a half years on Sprague Avenue. Took in cash, answered telephone, and I knew everybody up and down the street.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I worked there two and a half to three years, I guess. I liked the work, too, just fine. I did like to meet the public.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: This was before you were married?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, yes. Then, after I was married, we moved to a place over on Sharp Avenue and I raised chickens and flowers and sold them. I come down to our ranch and I raised over 800 geese. Like I say, you know, cured all the feathers and sold them and shipped the geese to Spokane.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I've got pictures of them.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What were the feathers used for?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Pillows and mattresses. I've got two feather mattresses. We've had feather mattresses and I gave each girl a pair of feather pillows, down pillows.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How do you cure feathers? Just dry them?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, the geese, I've always had them in a clean place, and when I kill them, see, I cut the shorter legs and then I catch the blood so it won't get on the feathers. Then, I take them and I freeze them. I'd run them through war water because you don't want to use detergent for goose feathers. Then, I freeze them dry.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Then I sell them for a dollar and a half [unintelligible] a pillow. That is a lot of work, too, I tell you. But, we used to get the big feathers and I couldn't be bothered with them. It was too many.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I had 35 to 40 geese every year and one year, I raised 69 and I killed them all and dressed them. That was just too much.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How did you seel them, then? Did people come to you and buy them?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. When the load got too heavy, why, they'd just call me up. I had a place in Spokane, The [unintelligible] Brothers and I used to send them about 30 geese up there every time [unintelligible]. Then I had ducks and turkeys and springers, and my pigs around town here.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I had regular customers. And butter customers, goodness, I used to sell 800 one pound [unin telligible] a year. Then I milked cows. I broke in some pretty kicky cows, I'm telling you, they had the mind, too.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Dad showed me how. They sure kicked the bucket out of my hand; but, most of them are pretty gently, you know. Every once in a while, you'll find one that's touchy and they should know, let them know you're boss.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I'll bet you could, tool

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, I did, I sure did.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And that's mostly what you did until you were married?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, in Spokane, I had raised flowers and I had a friend that run the cafeteria and she used to buy all the flowers from me. We raised a garden, three crops on three lots. I used to make sauerkraut, 15 gallon sauerkraut and sell that. So, I always had something to sell, something to turn over, you see.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: In the wintertime, you could find something to contribute.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, something that I could sell. Sometimes, I crocheted [unintelligible] or something, and I'd sell them. [Unintelligible] did an awful lot of cushion covers. I used to crochet those and sell them.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How long would it take you to make one?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, I don't, this was according to what size you'd get. The [unintelligible] would take a little longer because you have to stop and count everything, you know.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: About how much would you get for them?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, $3.50 to $5.00 [unintelligible].

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you had some income corning into the family all the time.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Uh huh. We've always managed to have something corning in, you know. When I raised fryers in Spokane, I had [unintelligible] all on the ground and they all had eggs. When the chickens hatched, I'd raise them all by hand.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I sold the fryers, you see. I had to have something to do. I couldn't stand to be idle.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Doesn't sound like you ever were.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I didn't [unintelligible] and didn't take it too easy.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You seem pretty spry now.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, after all the surgery I went through. They just did me all over again. I just had a good doctor, you know.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, good. You talked about your interests and hobbies and things. Did you ever have any kind of a hobby, just for fun?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I never thought about it. The days were never long enough to get through.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you didn't need anything just to take up the time.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. I sewed every stitch of clothing my girls wore until they was ten or twelve years old. I made their coats, even. I made all their stuff and in during when the times was tough, and people would give me their dresses and people in Spokane have pretty nice clothes, you know.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: They'd bring them home and cook the dye out of them and make them over. All of my girls sew, every one.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, you really trained them.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, they know how. Yeah, two of them made trips to Chicago on Four-H Club.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you have any organizations that you are a member of now?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: The Eastern Star.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Any thing else?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: And the Latah County Pioneers Association and the Museum of Moscow. I went to the Eastern Star. I was president and I was president of Latah County Pioneers. I was just in all that.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: But, I just can't, I think it was because of my hypertension bothered me too much, I can't take it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You are bothered with hypertension?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, I have high blood pressure. I got to be careful.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you just have to take it easy. Have you had any special awards? You showed me a ribbon you won. Was that Four-H?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, my Four-H was for the Latah County Museum, and I was hostess in a booth there. Let's see, I took eggs up there and onions and things at the fair, you know, from the ranch out there. We used to raise lots of corn and I used to buy a little section, and in the afternoon, they'd be twelve dozen a second. We used to take them down to Lewiston and get 20 cents a dozen.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Nice, yellow grain corn. Oh yeah, we had lots of nice corn and I had some fruit trees out there. Of course, that was on the other people's ground that my father had, he homesteaded that place.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Can you think of any other awards you've gotten?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. They called on me to give little talks in the Pioneer's Association and then they had them parades and things like that. They had a little old buggy with a top and the bottom had sled runners on it. They had wheels under that and they had me sitting on that.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I sat there and played the ruler organ. I had one of these ruler organs. I got it from my grandfather. It was about 78 years old.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That must have been something to see and hear .

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, I've been in the parades here. The last time I was in it, they had an amplifier on it and that way, you could hear it all over town. I like to take part in those kind of things. But the younger people, they do better tha·n I can.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What are some advantages and disadvantages you think there are in living in a small town like this?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, I don't know. I don't see anything wrong with it. I always get along. I get along with everybody in the area.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: There's [unintelligible] new people that come in, you know. Most everybody here owns their homes. But, I don't know too many people anymore. New people come in.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: So many of my friends have passed on, now.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It's a little harder for you to get out.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh yeah, it's harder for me. You get accustomed to it, you know, just like everything. I had one friend that come out to California several times and my daughter was living down there, and her daughter was. Ethel and I enjoyed [unintelligible]; it's lovely.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I have relatives down there and I had Christmas down there. But that's the only vacations I ever had. I always had to work.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you feel like life on a farm or in a rural community is better than in the city?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, you have to like farming. I always liked the open air and being independent. It's independent there, anyhow. I liked the city.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I know how to live there and I know how to get along with people. Then, on the farm, why, it's kind of a lonely life. Sometimes, you miss your friends. But, I liked the animals, I've always had success.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I've raised a garden. The bees used to be a problem and they'd sting a goose and I'd hear them, they'd squeal like a pig. I'd run out and put soda on it for a half hour and get the poison out of it and get the stinger out. If the stinger wasn't out, they would die, you know.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: And many a pig, the little pigs, oh, all the pigs I've had. Why, I used to take them when they was dead and set them down there under the stove and bring them back to life and raise them up, and get $50 or $60 out of them. And an apple box, I found out a way, too, you know. You put them in a box, you're always raising the top off.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Boy, I found out you have an apple on the end and they'll remove the end and that's what I feed, you see. You've got to be careful not to overfeed, too, because they'd get in trouble, you know. But, I knew the nature of a hog, though. I knew the nature of all animals.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you've had experience living in town and country, both.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, yeah. I lived 42 years on the ranch and then I lived 12 and a half years in Spokane. Spokane is a nice place. It was pretty lonesome for me [unintelligible], you know.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I missed the public often, much at first. But, there was a friend of mine that was sick quite a bit and I used to take care of her store. I run it forty--two days while she [unintelligible] in Spokane and it all come back to me how many people I hadn't seen in over 30 years ..

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And they remembered you.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, and I remembered them, too. We talked about things, you know. I really liked it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How about a woman, say, you lived in Spokane and on the farm too. I guess you pretty much decide what ...

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, you have to. See, we lived on a farm until I was about ten years old. You got to know something about animals and things because you go in there and you don't know the first thing about anything, and it's pretty hard. You have to under stand the nature of animals.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I learned all of that before I ever left the ranch. Then, my folks moved to town in the house up here on the corner and we had a cow and calves, and I went out to work, so I didn't come back anymore. I stayed out at work all the time.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You are pretty much alone, aren't you, now?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah. Well, my daughter comes up here and she calls me up every morning, and the girls in Seattle, they call me, too. They both call me. The oldest girl, now, she's 59, I think.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: When you were a child, compared to now, do you think children now have, of course, they have more money to do things with, don't they?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, yes, they do have. But, still, in them days, [unin- telligible] pennies, you know. [Unintelligible] know what pennies were. But, then they could come in [unintelligible], anybody give me a nickel or a dime and I thought I had a million, you know, and I'd be awful tickled about anything like that. They didn't have very much money, and when we'd go to the grocery store, Mother would take butter and eggs and trade them and pay for it.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I know she didn't have enough cash. She had to work pretty hard.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You spent most of your time working. Did you have any free time when you were young?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: [Unintelligible], I always had to work [unintelligible].

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Were your sisters, did they all go to school about the same time?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, they all went to school and graduated. They're all scattered. There's one in Lewiston .and there's one in Seattle.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did they go farther in school than you did?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I think they did. I don't remember.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What do you think you remember about your courtship and early married lif e? Where did you meet your husband?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I met him in Spokane.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you go out and have dates, or what did you do?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I was at a cashier's desk and he used to come in all the time. He come in one evening and asked me to go out. So we went out and we kept going together and then we got married.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: About how long did you go together?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, I don't know. I can't remember, that seemed quite a while ago. I got married when I was about pretty near 20.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Can you remember some of the reasons why you got married?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. Oh, my health broke down, that was one thing. I wasn't very well, my health broke down. He had a ... he had his mind on a little house out on Tenth Avenue and [unintelligible].

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: We went around and looked at it and then we finally got married. A nice little home.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What did you kind of expect marriage to be?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, I don't know. I didn't think nothing about it. I just thought everybody else did the same thing, so I just went along and we got along all right.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Would you have ever considered not getting married?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. I don't know. I just didn't pay much attention to it. I just went along in life, you know, I took life as it comes. [Unintelligible] my sisters come as long as we had a home there.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: They used to come and stay with me [unintelligible].

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did marriage turn out to be pretty much what you expected?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, it was all right, yeah, it was all right. I didn't have any discomforts or anything. Everything was all right. [Unintelligible.]

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It worked pretty much for you?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What medical services were available to you when you had your children?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I was in the maternity wards in the hospitals.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That was in Spokane?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I had two in Spokane and one in Colfax. Oh, I could never stay home, I near ly died in Colfax. I was never very well

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, it was fortunate that you were living in areas where you had doctors. Some women didn't have doctors in those days, did they?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, no. That's what killed my grandmother, you know, my mother, too. [Unintelligible}, her baby was born. She died and left the baby in Moscow. It was only four days old.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: She was the second one buried in the Moscow cemetery, in 1874.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Is that right? Where did you find out about how to raise children? Did you get advice about having the babies?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I got it from the doctor. I was going to a doctor, and I had a friend that was [unintelligible} and we always chummed together. We always got along fine.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you kind of shared ...

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: And the children all turned out to be all right. My sons in-law aren't too [unintelligible]. They don't drink and they don't chase. So they are pretty good guys.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, your daughters made pretty good marriages, then?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh yes, I don't complain. They always minded me pretty good, you know.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Was your mother near at hand, then?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, she was up in Canada.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you were pretty much on your own and with your own friends?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I was always on my own.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Are you pretty well satisfied with the way your girls turned out?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, yeah. They got good men and I couldn't complain. I don't complain at all. They are awful good to me.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: My sons-in law, they do everything they can for me. One of them, he's a teacher for retarded children in Seattle. They have two children, one is 20 and the other is 16.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Are most of your grandchildren in school now?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, yes. I have six great grandchildren.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Six grandchildren!

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Six grandchildren and six great grandchildren.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What do you think about the future for girls now, compared to when you grew up?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, I don't know. It depends on the ... the trouble nowadays is that parents are not companionship enough to their children.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You feel that way?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I think so. Look at the boys now. My son-in-law, he's got an awful nice boy over there in Seattle and he always went to school with them. He's a great companion to them.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: He's just a wonderful boy. Then, down in Colton, my oldest grandson, he just got his MD in agronomy. Then, he, oh, they got some trade with some company back East with seed and everything. They plant these flowers and they ship them by the ton and they pay for artificial flowers.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: They got two children. I got some valen tines from their little kids. Cute little children. They mind, too, believe me, they have to mind.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Pappy said the word and that's it. And then [unintelligible] running the dairy and they have to have help with them. And then, they have milking machines under 34 cows. I could always milk cows; but, I learned not on the milking machine, so I had my granddaughter show me how.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Then you could have that experience, too.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes. I wanted to know everything.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It sounds like they're keeping their children pretty busy.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, yes. They keep them busy. Like Mary says, [unintel ligible] ski patrol, great skier. He's working for the building [unintelligible] on the [unintelligible] yards [unintelligible].

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: He's a nice boy, too, don't smoke or drink either.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What do some of the girls plan to do?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: The granddaughters?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Uh huh.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh my goodness, one of them is married and she's on the staff at WSU. She works at the science department in agronomy. And then, the second one, she's married and her and her husband live in Clarkston. Then, she took a course in Georgia while he was stationed there, on catering.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Then, when they were only there two years, why, she catered to the personnel. She made a whole big money serving banquets and things. She has two children. And now, she gets a chance to serve a banquet, when she's called out, she makes $50 or $60 in the evening.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It sounds like your granddaughters are taking after you in keeping busy.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, yes, they like to be doing something.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you have friends come in for recreation?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Some people come and pick me up and I stop in Moscow at the rest home. Then I go to the doctor in Pullman all the time, I gotta go.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you read? Can you read now?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, it bothers my eyes. I used to love to do handwork, all crochet and, my, I did a lot of handwork.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you have television or radio?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I have television, radio, I have everything I want to hear.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you still don't have time on your hands.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I can sit around here and look out the window and people around town here call me up. I can't walk downtown any more like I used to. I'm getting too old for that, I guess.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: When your family was together, what kinds of things did you do for recreation?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, we had all kinds of pets, Shetland ponies [unintelligible]. We had pets of every kind. [Unintelligible.]

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, mostly they found their recreation around home?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, yes. They always stayed close to home. They didn't run around much. Everytime I came home, they were there.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That's important, isn't it?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You always knew where they were.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes. [Unintelligible] they could call me up and tell me [unintelligible].

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You've already told me a lot about how you helped support the family . Can you think of any other way you helped?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. My husband used to farm and he made good as he stayed with it. He worked awful hard, you know. I had 120 of my own, then, and we farmed 180 acres for my sister for a while.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: We had the 120, so I had somethi~g to sell all the time. I made cottage cheese and I canned corn and I'd sell something all the time. [Unintelligible.]

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You built the house by yourself?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. [Unintelligible.]

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You bought the lumber?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I bought the lumber from the [unintelligible]. My husband helped and then he worked, too.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: But you planned it.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, I planned everything. I was used to the farm and I managed, and if things weren't going just right, I [unintelligible].

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did this include your husband, too?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah. He wanted to, he had hogs, you know, and he'd milk cows.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Was there ever a time when you had the major responsibility of supporting the family?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: He was always there.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, he was always there. But, I [unintelligible] and everything.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you ever wonder or worry what might happen if some thing would happen to your husband?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I knew I always made my way ever since I was 15 years old, and if anything happened to him I could get along someway. I could always manage, you know. One time, I got hailed out and lost all our crop and everything. So he wanted to sell out for $4,000 and go to California.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Why, I said that I've got all this land here and I've got all that canned stuff and we got our milk cows and our hogs and calves and everything, and if you can find anything better in California, go and find it. Then I'll break up here, but not till then. And that just settled it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That was the last you heard of that.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah. That [unintelligible] thing to do, of course. I'd sell the farm for a good price, you see.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you still own some now?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, just this place here is mine now.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you do any, what you call community and church activities?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I didn't do anything [unintelligible].

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That was your organization.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And you're still kind of involved in that?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh yeah, pretty much so.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Have you ever, well, you've told me that you've displayed things in county fairs.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You've won ribbons and awards for that?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, and so have my children, too.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What suggestions would you give to a young woman who is starting out now and getting married and going to live out on a farm?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, I've never thought about that. It would be kind of hard to answer. It's pretty hard for a woman who has never lived on a farm. It's an awful mess of a business in itself.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, it's better if you_ grow up in it.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: It's a business in itself. Because even if a husband does know something, why, some of these fellows don't like to do any  thing. [Unintelligible] I know how to milk cows and how to do everything and I can do anything like that.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you were really half the partnership?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, and I could make a pig mind, too. I didn't monkey around with them at all.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you take any magazines or newspapers?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I take the Tribune, Genesee News, and the Moscow paper. I was taking the Review for a while. When I redo furniture, I redid all my furniture, I did that table and that sideboard and took all the varnish off and reupholstered that chair there.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How long ago did you do this? Just lately have you done this?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. Last year, I [unintelligible] in there, and my husband . got that secondhand. I always wanted a round table and it was $65 when we were first married and I thought we couldn't afford it. So, after I come down here, why, I went around to all the secondhand stores and I seen this one for $6, and I bought it and took all the varnish off.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: We were admiring the [unintelligible] on it.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah. It's worth $250. My daughter in Seattle said she wants that table. [Unintelligible] old-fashioned dresser [unintelligible] one daughter owns that. Then, I got a dresser with a great big mirror [unintelligible], so that's settled.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And you did that just this last year?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Two years ago. I picked up that chair and I paid $5 for that tapestry and I got something [unintelligible]. Back there, [unintelligible] all torn. So, I just took it apart and rebuilt it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It's beautiful!

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, everybody admires it. I've got some more chairs up stairs that I could fix, you know, but I don't have the strength in my hands anymore.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did you say you have a TV?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you have a favorite program?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, ''Lawrence Welk," and some of them educational programs . That's all [unintelligible].

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You still like animals.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh yes, I always did like them. You just have to under stand their nature.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What kind of things during your married life has your husband asked you for advice?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, nothing that I know of. We'd have our discussion when we bought our home in Spokane [unintelligible]. And, I don't know, we just kind of worked together. I had an awful lot of company all the time in this house in Spokane.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: People would come down and buy a lot of stuff from me.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Would they stay overnight?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, they'd just drive down for the day.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: But, usually, you and your husband made the family decisions together?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh yes, sure we did. He got the horses for the children, you know, [unintell~gible]. She could break them to [unintel ligible] had to mind her.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So they learned a lot of skills.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh yes, they were handy. They know how to can and how to sew and everything, and do things for themselves. I always taught them [unintelligible] you never know [unintelligible] grow up and [unintelligible] become a farmer, comes in handy with animals and everything.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: When you decided to leave Spokane and come back here to the farm, what was involved in it?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, my father gave us an offer and he told us to come down and farm [unintelligible]. There was 240 acres. He farmed it all the time.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, it really was an opportunity.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, it was an opportunity. I knew what I had to do and, of course, all he had to learn how to do was how to [unintelli gible] and manage the horses ...

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, it was new to him?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes. Well, he did in Pennsylvania, but, not much around here.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you just got into this business new and you helped him ...

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yes, I [unintelligible].

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, we've asked you about an awful lot of things, now. Is there anything else you'd like to tell us that we haven't covered?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I don't think there is anything else that I can think of.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: We were mostly asking about women on farms and what a woman's life has been like for you.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: One time, I set the incubator for 50 duck eggs and I got 44 little ducks. And one time, [unintelligible} these ducks, you know. So, I had these white [unintelligible] and I knew [unintelligible] around some place. I seen a wild [unintel ligible} hanging around the yard.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: So, in about 28 days, here come six little [unintelligible] out from under the house! That was kind of funny. And those skunks were terrible, you know, they would, and they'd sound terrible.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did they kill a lot of your animals?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh yeah, in the chicken house. They'd_ get them by their throat and suck the blood out. One time, I had a head of goose [unintelligible] out by the chicken house and bring the gander out there. I thought I heard them one morning about two o'clock.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: It was awful dark. So I had two good dogs and I heard the old . goose holler just once, and then the gander. I went out there she was gone. So, the dogs were spotting a coyote on the side of the hill.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: So I just went out there in the dark and I touched the gander and I talked to the hen goose and I picked her up and I carried her into [unintelligible] followed me all the way home. I put her back on the [unintelligible]. [Unintelligible] back of the neck, you know, they chew the neck [unintelligible.] And you don't [unintelligible] and if they don't eat them, the bears will come down, they know. You have to bury them.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That's interesting. Did you trap skunks?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No. [Unintelligible] as far away as I could get. The boys would have to shoot them.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Have you ever done that?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, but [unintelligible], he shot them. We had a dog that let us know. I said, "Oh, there's something black in the meadow." We were quite a ways from it. I said, "I believe that skunk's hanging around here again, oh no.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: " So we had a dog [unintelligible]. And here come that dog from the chicken house and the chickens were all cackling and hollering. So, I said, "That skunk [unintelligible]. I don't know, I could try." So I went up there.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I had a flashlight and my sho~gun and one dog, she stayed on the porch, she was always afraid. But, Old Rex, he wasn't afraid. So, [unintelligible] so I turned the flashlight on and [unintelligible] ammunition, .I'd shoot  him. So, for a couple years after [unintelligible].

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, they smell terrible! If you just put your clothes, you might kill the smell.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I've heard of tomato juice.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Yeah, tomato juice and ketchup, or something, anything acid. They're worth something now. You can get $28 for a hide if you can catch one of them.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I didn't know that.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: My grandson does that. My granddaughter and grandson does that [unintelligible]. They made 60 some dollars last month.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, good for him. Were coyotes ever a problem?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh, yes. I seen them come along and_ grab a [unintelli- . gible] and run away with it. They're awful, you know, they're just mean. But, they keep out of your way.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: They keep a certain peace.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, this really has been very interesting. Do you have any questions you'd like to ask? It's been interesting listening to you.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: My grandfather, one time when he first come here [unin telligible]. He homesteaded out here in the [unintelligible] district and the prairie chickens were so thick, he'd put out a wagon box and [unintelligible] and there would be enough prarie chickens [unintelligible] down on them.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You'd have a meal of prairie chickens.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: And the Indians, they'd take the prairie chickens and they would smear mud butter all over them and cook on the bonfire and pull the feathers all off and inside and eat them that way.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So you didn't even have to prepare them ahead.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: No, I didn't have to, no.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Would you be interested in seeing the sketch [unintelli gible]? AHJ Sure.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: I hope I did a good job.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Oh my! [Unintelligible.] I look like I'm about a hundred years old. Very good, good drawing there.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, we certainly do appreciate you taking the time to talk to us and everything.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, I can show you ... [Narrator begins playing an old ruler organ.]

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Very nice!

words: I've never seen one of those before.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: I've got "Nelly Gray," and I've got "Annie Laurie."

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And this was "Turkey in the Straw." The whole thing is 78 years old.

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: My grandfather had that.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Where do you think it was made?

speaker: Agnes Hailey Jones
words: Well, I don't know. I don't know. He bought it, I remember that. I know, one time, he was up here in Dr.

words: S ___ 's home and had a [unintelligible] in coffee pot and the governor's wife was there. "Oh," she says, "I've got some of these gals, have one of these little organs and I've got three wheels." "Well," I said, "I've got three of mine, now, and I wouldn't . give you one of them either!" words: That is something that you would only see in a museum.

words: Oh, yeah. A fellow offered me $200, a fellow from California. He wanted to, he said, "I'll give you $200 for it." I said, "No, I've got all the wheels to it and it's in real good shape."

words: I'm sure you don't want to sell it. But, I'm sure you could get a lot more than $300.
